story.title: An update should not erase the past
paragraphs: Correcting a false fact and updating a once-true fact are different operations: when a leader changes, the old and new answers are both correct for different dates. The paper calls the second case Temporal Knowledge Editing (TKE). An editor can pass tests on the new answer, its paraphrases, and unrelated facts while erasing the earlier one, because locality tests do not check the edited fact's history.

The new benchmark, AToKe (Assessment of TempOral Knowledge Editing), asks explicit-time questions, such as who held a position in a given span, and relative-time questions, such as who held it previously. The latter require an ordered history rather than isolated date–answer pairs.

mechanism.title: METO edits the outgoing fact and its time span
paragraphs: METO (Multi-Editing with Time Objective) first queries the model for the fact it currently holds, then edits that fact together with the newer ones, closing its time span and moving its wording to the past. Older facts are not replayed; the authors assume the model already treats them as history.

A second objective reverses the usual query: besides supplying the object for a dated relation, the model is edited to predict the time span of a given fact. METO runs both objectives through an existing editor, constrained fine-tuning (CFT), MEND, ROME, or MEMIT, so each comparison holds the editor fixed.

AToKe has three subsets: a single edit (SE), multiple successive edits of the same fact (ME), and an extending edit (EE) that prolongs a fact's validity. Scores cover current and historical facts under explicit-time questions (CES, HES), relative-time questions (CRS, HRS), and paraphrased current questions (CES-P); HES* asks every historical question after the last edit. Baseline prompts carry timestamps too, so their failures are not due to a missing date.

evidence.title: METO recovers some history at a cost to current accuracy
paragraphs: Without METO, every editor nearly erases history: single-edit HES is at most 2.41%, and HES* after multiple edits at most 0.27%. With METO, HES* exceeds 15% for every editor except CFT. Retention is not free: under single edits, METO lowers paraphrased (CES-P) and relative-time (CRS) current accuracy for all four editors.

Two difficulty patterns hold with and without METO: relative-time questions are harder than explicit-time ones, likely because they require ordering facts rather than recalling dates, and repeated edits are harder than a single one.

demo.title: Two timestamped edits, one question at a time
demo.description: Play the record's two edits in order. Each question form's probe and expected answer follow from the record, and the request panel shows what an existing editor and METO are asked to learn at that edit.

evidence.title: Which question forms does METO recover?
evidence.description: Choose an edit sequence, a question form, and an editor to compare measured accuracy without METO (Table 2) and with it (Table 3). All four editors stay visible for the chosen form.
